COMPTROLLER’S DECISION

This decision is considered final on February 12, 2024, unless a motion for rehearing is timely filed; this date of finality is calculated based on the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).[1] The failure to timely file a motion for rehearing may result in adverse legal consequences.

Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Keneshia Washington of the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) issued a Proposal for Decision (PFD) that includes Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law. SOAH served the PFD on each party and each party was given an opportunity to file exceptions and replies with SOAH in accordance with SOAH’s rules of procedure. The ALJ recommended that the Comptroller adopt the PFD as written.

After review and consideration, IT IS ORDERED that the PFD is adopted as written.

The result from this Decision is Attachment A. The ALJ’s recommendation letter is Attachment B. The PFD as written is Attachment C. Attachments A, B, and C are incorporated by reference.

Attachment A reflects a liability.

SOAH Docket No. 304-24-00252

TCPA Hearing No. 119,947

**************

Permit No. **************

v.

TEXAS COMPTROLLER OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS

Proposal for Decision

The Criminal Investigation Division (CID) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) determined that an employee of ************** (Petitioner), violated statutory regulations and sold e-cigarettes or tobacco products to a person younger than 21 years of age. The CID issued a Notice of Violation for Cigarette/Tobacco Retailer Permit No. ************** (Tobacco Permit), held by Petitioner, imposing a $1,000 fine authorized under the Texas Health and Safety Code. Petitioner requested a hearing to dispute the imposition of the fine. In this Proposal for Decision, the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) recommends the fine proposed by the Tax Division (Staff) of the Comptroller be imposed.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred this case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on September 12, 2023, issued a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission. On September 22, 2023, ALJ Keneshia Washington issued an Order Setting Written Submission Hearing, setting the hearing and establishing the record closing date of December 18, 2023. Teresa Gutierrez represented Staff, and ************** represented Petitioner.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction; therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE

Petitioner did not submit evidence for the hearing. Staff offered the following exhibits:

1. Notice of Violation No. XXXXX; and

2. CITY Municipal Court Citation and Complaint.

The exhibits were admitted without objection.

B. MATERIAL FACTS AND ISSUES PRESENTED

Petitioner operates a retail store in CITY, Texas. Petitioner is a tobacco retailer and sells cigarettes and other tobacco products under its tobacco permit, issued by the Comptroller.

On July 19, 2022, INDIVIDUAL, Petitioner’s employee, sold tobacco products to a person younger than 21 years of age. After the conclusion of the sale, officers with the CITY Police Department issued a citation to INDIVIDUAL for selling tobacco products to a person younger than 21 years of age, and on August 15, 2022, INDIVIDUAL entered a plea of no contest to the offense. As a result, INDIVIDUAL was found guilty of a violation under Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.082 in the Municipal Court of the CITY in COUNTY, Texas.

On June 16, 2023, CID issued a formal Notice of Violation (Notice) to Petitioner stating Petitioner violated provisions of Chapter 161 of the Health and Safety Code and referencing the violation of July 19, 2022, committed by its employee, INDIVIDUAL. The Notice stated the Comptroller intends to impose a fine of up to $1,000 on Petitioner and provided Petitioner the opportunity to request a hearing on the matter. Petitioner returned the form indicating it wanted a hearing, and on September 6, 2023, Staff referred the matter to SOAH. Staff maintains that Petitioner is subject to disciplinary action and proposes the fine should be upheld. Petitioner did not submit argument or evidence for the written submission hearing.

C. ALJ ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATION

Staff is alleging statutory violations that warrant imposition of a penalty or other disciplinary action and must establish the violations by a preponderance of the evidence. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1204(g).

Texas issues permits to several types of tobacco dealers. A tobacco permit holder is defined as a bonded agent, distributor, wholesaler, manufacturer, importer, export warehouse, or retailer who obtains a permit under Texas Tax Code § 154.101. See Tex. Tax Code § 154.001(14). A tobacco retailer is defined as a person who engages in the business of selling cigarettes to consumers and includes the owner of a cigarette vending machine. See id. § 154.001(17). In this case, there is no dispute regarding the fact that Petitioner’s store was a tobacco retailer and held a tobacco permit at the time of the violation at issue.

Under the Texas Health and Safety Code, a person commits an offense (Class C misdemeanor) if the person, with criminal negligence, sells, gives, or causes to be sold or given a cigarette, e-cigarette, or tobacco product to someone who is younger than 21 years of age. See Tex. Health and Safety Code § 161.082(a)(1), (c). In addition to the possible criminal citation of an individual who makes the sale to a person younger than 21 years of age, a tobacco retailer is subject to disciplinary action if, as in this case, an employee of the retailer commits an offense under Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 161. See Tex. Health and Safety Code § 161.0901(a). If the Comptroller finds, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing as provided by Texas Government Code Chapter 2001, that a permit holder has violated Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 161 at a place of business for which a permit is issued, the Comptroller may suspend the permit for that place of business and administratively assess a fine. See id. § 161.0901(b). For the first violation during the 24-month period preceding the violation at that place of business, the Comptroller may require the permit holder to pay a fine in an amount not to exceed $1,000. See id. § 161.0901(b)(1). The statutory scheme imposes strict liability, so that if the agent or employee of the retailer is found to have committed an offense under Chapter 161, the retailer is liable for sanction noticed under Section 161.0901.

The ALJ finds Staff demonstrated, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Petitioner’s employee, INDIVIDUAL, was cited for and found guilty of the offense of selling cigarettes, e-cigarettes, or tobacco products to a person younger than 21 years of age in violation of the Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.082(a)(1). Therefore, Petitioner was subject to disciplinary action, including a fine, under Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.0901. Because Petitioner violated Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 161 at a place of business for which the tobacco permit was issued, the Comptroller noticed Petitioner of the violation and of the proposed $1,000 fine and provided Petitioner the opportunity for a hearing. See id. § 161.0901(b). Considering the evidence in the contested case record, the $1,000 fine against Petitioner should be upheld.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. ************** (Petitioner) operates a retail store in CITY, Texas.

2. Petitioner is a tobacco retailer and sells cigarettes and other tobacco products under its tobacco permit issued by the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller).

3. On July 19, 2022, INDIVIDUAL, Petitioner’s employee, sold tobacco products to a person younger than 21 years of age.

4. After the conclusion of the sale, officers with the CITY Police Department issued a citation to INDIVIDUAL for selling tobacco products to a person younger than 21 years of age.

5. On August 15, 2022, INDIVIDUAL entered a plea of no contest to the offense, and as a result, INDIVIDUAL was found guilty of a violation under Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.082 in the Municipal Court of the CITY in COUNTY, Texas.

6. On June 16, 2023, the Criminal Investigation Division CID of the Comptroller issued a formal Notice of Violation (Notice) to Petitioner stating Petitioner violated provisions of Chapter 161 of the Health and Safety Code and referencing the violation of July 19, 2022, committed by its employee, INDIVIDUAL.

7. The Notice stated the Comptroller intends to impose a fine of up to $1,000 on Petitioner and provided Petitioner the opportunity to request a hearing on the matter.

8 Petitioner returned the form indicating it wanted to have a hearing regarding the noticed violation and fine.

9. On September 6, 2023, the Tax Division (Staff) of the Comptroller referred the matter to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH).

10. On September 12, 2023, Staff issued Petitioner a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission. The notice contained a statement of the nature of the hearing; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearing was to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaint or petition filed with the state agency.

11. On September 22, 2023, the Administrative Law Judge issued an order setting the written submission hearing.

12. Petitioner did not submit evidence or argument for the written submission hearing.

13. The record closed December 18, 2023.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over this matter. Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to this hearing, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearing. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Health and Safety Code § 161.0901.

4. Staff must establish the violation(s) at issue by a preponderance of the evidence. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1204(g).

5. Texas issues permits to several types of tobacco dealers. A tobacco permit holder is defined as a bonded agent, distributor, wholesaler, manufacturer, importer, export warehouse, or retailer who obtains a permit under Texas Tax Code § 154.101. See Tex. Tax Code § 154.001(14).

6. A tobacco retailer is defined as a person who engages in the business of selling cigarettes to consumers and includes the owner of a cigarette vending machine. See Tex. Tax Code § 154.001(17).

7. Under the Texas Health and Safety Code, a person commits an offense (Class C misdemeanor) if the person, with criminal negligence, sells, gives, or causes to be sold or given a cigarette, e-cigarette, or tobacco product to someone who is younger than 21 years of age. See Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.082(a)(1), (c).

8. In addition to the possible criminal citation of an individual who makes the sale to a person younger than 21 years of age, a tobacco retailer is subject to disciplinary action if, as in this case, an employee of the retailer commits an offense under Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 161. See Tex. Health and Safety Code § 161.0901(a).

9. If the Comptroller finds, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing as provided by Texas Government Code Chapter 2001, that a permit holder has violated Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 161 at a place of business for which a permit is issued, the Comptroller may suspend the permit for that place of business and administratively assess a fine. See Tex. Health and Safety Code § 161.0901(b).

10. For the first violation during the 24-month period preceding the violation at that place of business, the Comptroller may require the permit holder to pay a fine in an amount not to exceed $1,000. See Tex. Health and Safety Code § 161.0901(b)(1).

11. Staff established, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Petitioner’s employee, INDIVIDUAL, was cited for and convicted of selling cigarettes, e-cigarettes, or tobacco products to a person younger than 21 years of age in violation of the Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.082(a)(1).

12. Due to the violation by INDIVIDUAL, Petitioner was subject to disciplinary action, including a fine, under Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.0901.

13. The Comptroller noticed Petitioner of the violation and of the proposed $1,000 fine and provided Petitioner the opportunity for a hearing. See Tex. Health and Safety Code § 161.0901(b).

14. The $1,000 fine against Petitioner should be upheld.

SIGNED December 19, 2023

KENESHIA WASHINGTON

PRESIDING ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE
